{{short description|Jewish mathematician and astronomer}}
'''Itzḥak ben Shlomo ibn al-Aḥdab''' (or '''ibn al-Ḥadib''') '''ben Tzaddiq ha-Sefardi''' ({{langx|he|יצחק בן שלמה בן צדיק אלאחדב הספרדי}}, c. 1350 – c. 1426) was a [[Jew]]ish mathematician, astronomer, and poet.<ref>{{cite book|editor-first=Ora|editor-last=Raanan|language=Hebrew|location=Lod|year=1988|title=The Poems of Iṣḥak ben Shlomo Al-Aḥdab|publisher=Mekhon Haberman le-meḥḳere sifrut}}</ref>

Ibn al-Aḥdab was born in [[Castile (historical region)|Castile]] to a prominent Jewish family. He was a student of Judah ben Asher II, the great-grandson of [[Asher ben Jehiel|Asher ben Yeḥiel]] of Cologne, who was killed in the [[History of the Jews in Spain#1300–1391|anti-Jewish massacres]] of 1391. By 1396 Ibn al-Aḥdab had fled Spain and was in [[Sicily]], where he lived (in [[Syracuse, Sicily|Syracuse]] and [[Palermo]]) until his death around 1426.<ref>{{cite book|first=M.|last=Steinschneider|title=Mathematik bei den Juden|edition=2|publisher=Hildensheim|year=1964|page=168|language=German}}</ref>

== Work ==
He studied the algebra of Maghrebi mathematician [[Ibn al-Banna' al-Marrakushi|Ibn al-Bannā]] and published ''The Epistle of the Number'', a translation and detailed commentary on Ibn al-Bannā's 13th century treatise ''Talḵīṣ ʿAmal al-Ḥisāb'' ("A summary of the operations of calculation").<ref name=katz>{{cite journal|first=Victor|last=Katz|author-link=Victor J. Katz|title=The Mathematical Cultures of Medieval Europe|journal=History and Pedagogy of Mathematics|year=2016|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01349229/document}}</ref> The work is notable in being the first known Hebrew-language treatise to include extensive algebraic theories and operations.<ref>{{cite book|last=Wartenberg|first=Ilana|title=The epistle of the number, by Ibn al-Ahdab|series=Perspectives on Society and Culture|location=Piscataway|publisher=Gorgias Press|year=2015|isbn=978-1-4632-0417-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Reif|first=Stefan C.|title=Hebrew manuscripts at Cambridge University Library: a description and introduction|volume=52|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1997|isbn=978-0521583398}}</ref>

His astronomical works include ''Oraḥ selulah (Upraised Path)'', a set of tables in Hebrew for conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun and the Moon,<ref>{{cite journal|title=Isaac ibn al-Ḥadib and Flavius Mithridates: The Diffusion of an Iberian Astronomical Tradition in the Late Middle Ages|last1=Goldstein|first1=Bernard R.|last2=Chabás|first2=José|journal=Journal for the History of Astronomy|issn=0021-8286|volume=37|number=127|pages=147–172|year=2006|doi=10.1177/002182860603700202|url=http://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/2006JHA....37..147G|bibcode=2006JHA....37..147G|s2cid=220913612}}</ref> ''Keli Ḥemdah (Precious Instrument),'' which describes a unique [[equatorium]] of his own invention, functioning on the [[Ptolemaic epicycle|Ptolemaic theory of epicycles]],''<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Goldstein|first=Bernard R.|date=1987|title=Descriptions of Astronomical Instruments in Hebrew|url=https://nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1749-6632.1987.tb37198.x|journal=Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=500|issue=1|pages=105–141|doi=10.1111/j.1749-6632.1987.tb37198.x|bibcode=1987NYASA.500..105G |s2cid=84990297 |issn=1749-6632|url-access=subscription}}</ref>'' and ''Keli Memutsa (Intermediate Instrument)'', which describes another unique instrument of his own design, a combination [[astrolabe]]-[[Quadrant (instrument)|quadrant]]''.<ref name=":1" />'' [[Bernard R. Goldstein]] published a partial translation of ''Keli Ḥemdah'' in 1987.<ref name=":1" /> ''Oraḥ selulah'' survives in 25 MSS, ''Keli Ḥemdah'' in 15 MSS, and ''Keli Memutsa'' in 1 MS.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=HebrewBooks.org Sefer Detail: הגדה של פסח - פסח דורות -- אלאחדב, יצחק בן שלמה|url=https://hebrewbooks.org/50715|access-date=2021-03-19|website=hebrewbooks.org}}</ref> 

He is the author of a commentary on the [[Passover Haggada|Passover Haggadah]], titled ''Pesach Doros'' (''Passover of later generations)'' and printed by Mekhon Bet Aharon ṿe-Yiśraʼel in 2000.<ref name=":0" />

''Leshon ha-Zahav (Golden Language)'', an explication of the names for units and measurements found in the [[Hebrew Bible]].<ref name=":0" />

He is probably the author of a commentary on [[Maimonides]]' ''[[Mishneh Torah|Laws of the Sanctification of the Month]],'' found in the same MS as ''Leshon ha-Zahav'' with no author given.<ref name=":0" />

He also wrote songs, published as ''Shirei Rabbeinu Itzḥak ben Shlomo ibn al-Aḥdab'' (1987). He is known to have composed a work called ''Shir ha-Shirim,'' but it has not survived.<ref name=":0" />
